levels.name: SUNBREAK SHELF
levels.description: Sunlit approaches and a shallow seabed. Learn the return journey before the ocean closes in.

levels.name: GLASSBONE RIFT
levels.description: Tighter rock fields and the first Abyss Stalkers. Longer journeys reward careful preparation.

levels.name: DROWNED GARDENS
levels.description: The light disappears. Crimson Reapers patrol below 800 metres; sonar and boost become lifelines.

levels.name: MIDNIGHT CATHEDRAL
levels.description: A long descent through crowded hunting grounds. Stronger shields, lamps and ordnance earn their keep.

levels.name: CALYPSO ABYSS
levels.description: The deepest seabed and the strongest hunters. Recover the final six recorders and finish the transmission.

records.title: Routine maintenance
records.speaker: ENGINEER MARA VENN · DAY 01
records.text:
The Shelf beacon is losing four seconds every hour. Nothing dramatic. A corroded reference crystal, probably. I have asked Calypso to send a clean clock pulse.

Someone has already answered. Three rising notes, then a voice asking us to keep the receiver open. Calypso says their transmitter is still in its shipping crate.

records.title: An earlier emergency
records.speaker: DISPATCHER IONA REED · DAY 03
records.text:
At 06:14 every station received the same distress call: "Do not shut the listening array down. There are people inside." We logged it as interference until the checksum matched a packet in our commissioning archive.

That packet was recorded eleven days before construction began. The director wants the timestamps corrected. I am keeping both copies.

records.title: Glassbone
records.speaker: GEOLOGIST DR SEN KORA · DAY 06
records.text:
The pale ribs are not glass. Under pressure the mineral layers store mechanical vibration and release it in order. A natural recording medium, larger than any instrument we brought.

We pinged the east wall this morning. It returned yesterday’s ping, followed by our own voices. We had not spoken into the hydrophone.

records.title: Missing hours
records.speaker: ENGINEER MARA VENN · DAY 08
records.text:
Our navigation network takes its time from Calypso. Calypso takes its time from the crystal seam. You can see the problem.

The "old" distress packet is not proof of a message from the future. It is proof that our clocks have been trusting the thing we are trying to measure. An independent mechanical clock is on its way down.

records.title: A map of quiet places
records.speaker: SURVEY PILOT ADA SLOANE · DAY 09
records.text:
The miners left charges along the fracture. Please stop calling them unexploded salvage. Give the chains room.

There is a route west of the main ribs where the echo falls away. Small fish gather there. Whatever is happening below, they seem to know where the water is quiet. I have marked the route for the evacuation boats.

records.title: The garden listens
records.speaker: BIOLOGIST NELL ARDEN · DAY 11
records.text:
The colonies close before a pressure pulse reaches our instruments. Their roots run through the seam; each colony is a little receiver.

No mind is speaking to us. Not yet. But the ocean is carrying impressions of things that happened elsewhere, and the gardens are responding. I wish the company would find that extraordinary enough.

records.title: The demonstration
records.speaker: DIRECTOR HALDEN ROE · DAY 12
records.text:
A continuous model of an entire sea. No cables. No moving parts. Every vibration stored and retrievable. That was the proposal.

The investors asked for a voice. I played them the distress fragment and told them it was a controlled test. I am recording this because I want the person who finds it to know exactly where the lie began.

records.title: Three notes
records.speaker: DISPATCHER IONA REED · DAY 13
records.text:
The three rising notes are our evacuation beacon, stretched by pressure. The voice belongs to Mara. She is alive. She has not said those words.

The independent clock agrees with our surface clock. The message is not old. It is repeating along paths of different lengths, then entering a network that has assigned every repeat the wrong date. A very convincing haunting.

records.title: Turn it down
records.speaker: BIOLOGIST NELL ARDEN · DAY 14
records.text:
The amplification test is frightening the animals. They leave the gardens in waves. The large hunters follow the noise, not the lights.

I asked for silence and received a revised schedule. We are building a loudspeaker in a habitat we barely understand. The gardens close every time it charges. They are not applauding.

records.title: The cathedral
records.speaker: SURVEY PILOT ADA SLOANE · DAY 15
records.text:
The chamber is natural. The columns are the old seam folded back into itself. We bolted our listening equipment to the only part that was still growing.

Something very large lives in the outer passage. It waits, listens, then commits to one violent line. When it misses, it has to turn its whole body. I came back with paint missing, but I came back.

records.title: Do not wake it
records.speaker: ENGINEER MARA VENN · DAY 15
records.text:
The observation buoy is on a separate circuit. Leave it alone unless you intend to meet the resident. Its test sequence sounds like a wounded animal.

There is nothing beyond that creature we need for evacuation. No recorder, no crystal quota. Curiosity is a choice. Please make it while you still have enough air to choose differently.

records.title: Inside
records.speaker: ENGINEER MARA VENN · DAY 16
records.text:
The elevator gates have lost power. Six of us are behind the inner maintenance bulkhead. The emergency release is driven by the listening array’s return circuit.

Do not shut the listening array down. There are people inside.

There. Now I have said it. Send that on the independent channel. Do not let another broken timestamp bury it.

records.title: The wrong rescue
records.speaker: DIRECTOR HALDEN ROE · DAY 16
records.text:
Surface control believed the call was an old test and ordered the array isolated. I signed the test report that convinced them.

Ada has gone below with a battery tow. I have opened every gate I can still reach. There is no elegant technical explanation for what I did. When the logs are recovered, leave my name on this one.

records.title: Last boat upward
records.speaker: SURVEY PILOT ADA SLOANE · DAY 17
records.text:
Six passengers. One spare battery. Far too much weight. Mara is taking the pump apart with a dinner knife and telling me to stop watching the depth gauge.

We are clear of the chamber. Calypso is still calling. Not because someone is trapped there now, but because we taught the stone to repeat an emergency. The animals do not know the difference.

records.chapter: The other end of the call
records.title: Calypso control
records.speaker: ENGINEER MARA VENN · AFTER EVACUATION
records.text:
Everyone from the inner bulkhead reached the surface. I am making this clear before the rest: everyone.

The array remains in automatic repetition. Cutting its power at the top would leave the pressure bank cycling for months. We need the original calibration records to identify the safe release sequence. They are spread across five stations.

records.chapter: The other end of the call
records.title: A stored ocean
records.speaker: GEOLOGIST DR SEN KORA · AFTER EVACUATION
records.text:
The seam stores impressions, not souls. It cannot distinguish a distress call from a passing shoal. We can choose what our machines amplify.

The quieting sequence does not erase the reef. It removes our repeating signal and lets the mineral return to its own slow conversation. That distinction matters.

records.chapter: The other end of the call
records.title: The cost of a signal
records.speaker: BIOLOGIST NELL ARDEN · AFTER EVACUATION
records.text:
We have a count of the people who survived. We do not have a count of the migrations we interrupted, or the hunting grounds we displaced.

When you return, watch the small fish. If they have begun to settle, that will tell us something the company’s dashboard cannot. You do not need to collect them. Let a living thing be enough.

records.chapter: The other end of the call
records.title: A pilot named Nereid
records.speaker: SURVEY PILOT ADA SLOANE · RECOVERY BRIEF
records.text:
They are fitting a little survey boat for the recorder run. NEREID. Narrow enough for the old service passages, stubborn enough for the pressure.

The pilot will get a list of equipment and a very tidy map. Tell them maps do not bring you home. Knowing when to turn around does. And leave a little room for the joy of seeing something no one else has seen.

records.chapter: The other end of the call
records.title: The release sequence
records.speaker: DISPATCHER IONA REED · RECOVERY BRIEF
records.text:
Twenty recorders carry the independent timing references. Together they let the harbour transmitter separate the real call from its returning copies.

No final switch in a monster’s mouth. No heroic sacrifice. Bring the records home, let the calibration finish, and we can stop asking the water to remember our worst day.

records.chapter: The other end of the call
records.title: Open water
records.speaker: ENGINEER MARA VENN · RECOVERY COMPLETE
records.text:
The correction is accepted. The repeaters are winding down. For the first time in weeks, the receiver has nothing urgent to say.

Thank you for bringing our voices back in the right order. The research stations can wait. There is still an ocean outside them.

NEREID, you are free to explore.
